summary:
Lunar Command: The Last Sunlight is a Moon survival game where you’re in charge of a lunar base and have to get it through a bunch of tough decisions. You only have so much battery power, and you have to split it between crew supplies, the storm shelter and science experiments. Meanwhile you’re getting ready for radiation storms and trying to keep everyone safe.

We made it for younger players, because space exploration can feel complicated or out of reach for kids. Pip is a friendly robot who helps you along the way. Pip explains what each resource does, gives you tips, and helps you understand what happened because of your choices. Before you do anything you can preview what it’ll change, so you can try out different strategies. You learn from what works and from what goes wrong.

Our project fits the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge because it takes big ideas like lunar habitats, managing resources and space exploration and turns them into something kids can actually play and learn from. We think that matters because it gets kids curious and thinking through problems themselves. It also shows the next generation how hard it really is to keep people alive away from Earth.
details:
Lunar Command is a browser game where you play as the commander of a small base on the Moon, and your job is to keep the base and its crew alive. Basically, the game is split into mission shifts. In each shift you decide what to do with a limited amount of battery power: keep the crew stocked with supplies, build up the storm shelter, or run science experiments. You usually can’t do all of them, so you have to pick.

Most of the game is about managing resources, and every choice affects something else. Before you commit to an action you can preview what it will do. After each shift you can see how your resources changed and adjust your plan. Radiation storms show up and add pressure, so you have to get the shelter ready ahead of time. If you mess up, the game doesn’t just tell you “wrong.” You see what happened because of your choice, and I think that’s a better way to learn.

Our favourite part is Pip, a friendly little robot who helps you through the mission. Pip explains words or ideas you might not know, answers questions about your resources, gives hints when you’re stuck, and explains why some decisions matter more than others. At the end you get feedback on your mission and your results, so you can look back at what you did.

We built the game with React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML and CSS. The game logic and the resource system is in TypeScript to keep it organised. We used React for the interface and the reusable components, and Vite for running it during development and building the final version. We also wrote automated tests for the game mechanics. They check that actions are valid, that resource calculations are right, and that the preview of an action matches what actually happens when you take it. That last one caught a few bugs. The game is live as a public website on Netlify.

What makes Lunar Command creative is that it mixes a game, real decision-making and a character who teaches you. It doesn’t hand you a list of space facts. It puts you in the position of actually running a lunar base, so you feel how hard it is. Pip makes it less intimidating, and the mission setup makes you want to try different strategies and see what works.

While we were building it we thought a lot about accessibility, using language that suits younger players, keeping the controls simple, and making sure the layout works on different screen sizes. The hardest part was explaining complicated ideas in a simple way without making them so simple that you stop learning anything. we also made the gameplay deterministic: the same decision always gives the same result, so players can understand why things happen and it never feels random.

We hope Lunar Command gets younger kids interested in computer science, engineering and space, and helps them practise problem-solving, critical thinking and managing limited resources along the way. In the end, we wanted to show how hard it is to keep people alive away from Earth, and make it fun and exciting to figure out.
